video_title: "No Signs Of The A.I. Party Slowing Down" | Craig Fuller
gist: FreightWaves CEO Craig Fuller says freight data shows a K-shaped economy: consumer goods volumes (food & bev hit by GLP-1s, SNAP limits, immigration-driven population degrowth; housing/remodeling) are slowing, while industrials are at a decade high, driven chiefly by AI data center capex plus cheap US natural gas and defense spending, with no sign of an AI capex slowdown. The New Harbor segment counters with AI-bubble risk (GPU inventories, Meta negative cash flow), notes cut equity exposure and defensive rotation, and frames the 8-9 month precious-metals drawdown as a 2008-style pullback.

themes.theme: K-shaped freight economy: consumer goods rolling over

insights.claim: Craig Fuller describes himself as 'lukewarm' on the US economy: freight data shows consumer goods volumes slowing while industrial categories expand, a reversal of the COVID-era consumer-led economy.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Consumer-exposed goods sectors face volume headwinds even as industrials boom.
insights.quote: In the data, it tells us that the consumer has slowed down their consumption of physical goods.

insights.claim: Fuller argues freight volumes are a cleaner demand signal than government data or same-store retail sales because inflation inflates nominal sales, while shippers only move goods when real demand exists.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Use unit/volume freight data rather than nominal sales to gauge real consumption.
insights.quote: When we look at freight data, people only move product when there's demand to actually drive it.

insights.claim: Fuller says freight data typically leads broader government economic data by about six months.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Freight indicators can serve as an early-warning system for macro turns.
insights.quote: the freight data is usually 6 months before the broader uh government data

insights.claim: Freight volume tracks population and units consumed, not dollars spent: a $100 steak and a $10 chicken are both 'a unit of one', so consumer goods volumes can fall even while dollar spending holds up.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Divergence between nominal retail sales and real volumes is a hidden consumer weakness signal.

insights.claim: Food and beverage is a major laggard, with a 'pretty sharp slowdown' in volume consumption, notable because snack and beverage consumption actually rose during the Great Financial Crisis.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Weakness in a historically recession-resistant category suggests structural, not cyclical, drivers.
insights.quote: Food and beverage is actually a pretty big laggard right now.

insights.claim: Fuller attributes the food & beverage volume slowdown to four factors: population degrowth from curtailed immigration, SNAP restrictions on unhealthy products, shrinkflation reducing shipped weight, and GLP-1 drug adoption.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Packaged food/beverage and snack makers face multiple simultaneous volume headwinds.

insights.claim: Fuller believes GLP-1 drugs are a much bigger deal for food demand than most people believe; reverse-logistics companies report food products sitting on shelves longer, and with 10+ million users the effect shows up in data.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Underappreciated structural headwind for processed food, snacks and beverage volumes.
insights.quote: I think the GLP-1 factor is a much bigger deal than most people believe it is.

insights.claim: GLP-1 users shift budget from food and beverage to clothing and apparel as they change sizes, so apparel volumes are robust; since most apparel is imported, import freight is strong while domestic food freight weakens.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Apparel retailers and import logistics may benefit from GLP-1 adoption at food's expense.

insights.claim: Roughly 95% of calories consumed in the US are domestically produced, so Fuller argues tariffs are not actually driving food prices.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Food inflation narratives tied to tariffs are overstated per Fuller.
insights.quote: Like 95% of the calories we consume

insights.claim: Up to about 20% of US freight volume is indirectly related to housing (construction, appliances, furniture, TVs, paint), and housing weakness is a substantial drag on freight.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Housing-linked goods manufacturers and carriers remain under pressure.
insights.quote: as much as 20% of the volume of freight in the United States is indirectly related to housing

insights.claim: Housing is weakening further, including the remodeling segment: post-COVID locked-in homeowners (e.g., 2.7% mortgages) remodeled instead of moving through about 2024, but that remodeling wave has now exhausted itself over the last two years.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Home improvement and furnishings demand lacks a near-term catalyst.

insights.claim: Building-materials contacts tell Fuller interest rates are a factor but not the primary reason people aren't buying homes; overall cost of living and housing affordability is.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Rate cuts alone may not revive housing demand.
insights.quote: they'll tell you that interest rates are a factor, but they're not the primary reason that people aren't buying homes.

insights.claim: The US overbuilt multifamily housing, landlords are offering big incentives, and Fuller sees potential for a multifamily debt crisis that is only held off because people can't afford to buy homes.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Multifamily lenders/REITs carry latent credit risk if home affordability improves.

insights.claim: Freight is priced at the margin like oil's 'incremental barrel'; consumer freight dropping only a couple percent signals a mediocre consumer freight economy that should be much stronger given strong industrial activity.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Small marginal volume changes carry outsized signal value.
insights.quote: It's the same thing in freight. It's the incremental load of I have to move it and I'll pay whatever.

themes.theme: Industrial renaissance drivers: energy, defense, AI capex

insights.claim: Fuller calls the current US industrial economy the strongest in perhaps a decade, after being 'a dog' since roughly 2015-2017; the rebound began around November of last year.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Industrials have decoupled to the upside from a weak consumer.
insights.quote: I would say this is the strongest industrial economy that we have seen in in perhaps a decade

insights.claim: The industrial expansion is disintermediated from the consumer: traditional US manufacturing lifeblood (food & bev, autos, housing) is weak, while the boom comes from energy, defense and AI capex.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Industrial strength is not a read-through to consumer health.

insights.claim: Fuller identifies three primary drivers of US industrial activity: the AI data center capex boom (the biggest), cheap and available US energy, and military/defense spending; reshoring from tariffs is a factor but not the driver.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Position for capex, energy-intensive manufacturing and defense rather than tariff-driven reshoring.
insights.quote: So, reshoring is a factor but not the driver.

insights.claim: Contrary to the textbook view, Fuller argues high global energy prices are good for US industrials because US energy is relatively cheaper and available, so the world sources energy-derivative manufactured goods from the US.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Energy price spikes may widen US manufacturing cost advantage rather than hurt it.
insights.quote: high energy prices is a good thing for US industrial activity.

insights.claim: Fuller says US natural gas, not oil, is the real lifeblood of the US industrial economy, with domestic petrochemicals and products like polyester made from natural gas thanks to the shale revolution.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: US gas-advantaged chemicals and industrials benefit from structural cost edge.
insights.quote: It's US natural gas that's actually the lifeblood of the US industrial economy.

insights.claim: Energy is about 40% of product cost in heavy manufacturing, far more important than labor, so companies are relocating to the US because of energy rather than tariffs; Germany's decommissioning of energy production stunted its industrial might.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Energy-cost differentials favor US over European heavy industry.
insights.quote: 40% of heavy manufacturing is energy is 40% of the cost of of a product in heavy manufacturing.

insights.claim: Fuller argues war and defense spending are good for the US economy and industrial base because defense was never outsourced; he cites roughly 65% of global defense spending as American and 75-80% including allies who must buy American goods.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Defense manufacturing is a durable domestic industrial tailwind.

themes.theme: AI data center capex boom shows no slowdown

insights.claim: Fuller sees nothing in freight data suggesting any slowdown in AI capex spending, while acknowledging tail risks such as a CoreWeave bankruptcy or a failed Anthropic IPO.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Physical-economy data still supports continued AI build-out near term.
insights.quote: nothing in the data that suggests that this party is not going to continue.

insights.claim: Fuller argues AI capex differs from government stimulus because it is funded by cash flows of the most successful companies in history, and he believes reported revenues (e.g., SpaceX/xAI) are real.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Self-funded private capex is more durable than printed-money stimulus.

insights.claim: Railroads are the biggest transport beneficiaries of the AI data center build-out and a way to play AI with a real non-AI business underneath, as commodities and grid equipment for data centers move by rail.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Railroads offer AI capex exposure with downside protection from a core business.
insights.quote: if you want to invest in an AI stock and benefit from the AI data center build out the railroads are fantastic uh positions to own

insights.claim: Fuller believes the AI capex boom effectively bailed out the Trump administration's economy, which looked dire a year ago, while the administration credits tariffs.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Policy narrative overstates tariffs; an AI capex pullback would remove the main growth prop.
insights.quote: I think the AI capex boom in many ways bailed out the administration.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers serve as creditworthy anchor customers that let utilities finance new nuclear and natural gas plants, giving the economy power generation usable beyond data centers.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Data center demand underwrites grid and generation build-out for the wider economy.

insights.claim: Fuller claims electrifying every US vehicle would require far more power than AI data centers consume, so data-center-driven power build-out is a prerequisite for EVs and robotics.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Power generation is the binding constraint for multiple tech transitions.

insights.claim: New Harbor's John Lohr cites Fed data on investment in information-processing equipment and software as a share of GDP, warning that like the dot-com era IT spend AI spend may look unstoppable until it falls off a cliff.
insights.speaker: John Lohr (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Lagging physical data may not warn before an AI capex cliff.

insights.claim: Lohr points to anecdotes of GPUs piling up in inventory, neoclouds like CoreWeave building as long as financing is available, and Meta selling off after disclosing negative cash flow from AI equipment spending.
insights.speaker: John Lohr (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Watch neocloud financing and hyperscaler free cash flow as AI bubble stress signals.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart, citing Jan Van Eck, says compute demand still far outstrips supply, and argues the key tell for an AI cycle turn will be weakness at the margin in compute demand or transport volumes.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: Monitor compute demand and freight volumes before repositioning on AI.

insights.claim: Taggart, who leans toward AI being a bubble, warns against shorting it (a shot bull elephant can still trample for a long time) and recommends hedges for those who stay long.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: Risk-manage both directions rather than betting outright on an AI top.

themes.theme: Energy shock: diesel, Hormuz and Ukraine

insights.claim: Fuller says crude volumes through the Strait of Hormuz are at or near pre-war levels; the real problem is refined products, specifically diesel.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Refining margins and diesel availability matter more than crude flows.
insights.quote: It's not It's not crude that's the problem. It's the refined energies.

insights.claim: Fuller argues Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries are as important as Hormuz to the diesel crisis, explaining why the administration has grown harsh toward Zelenskyy; US diesel exports worsen domestic strain on farmers and truckers.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Diesel relief depends on Russia-Ukraine as much as Iran.

insights.claim: Fuller expects the status quo on diesel and energy to persist because neither the Iran nor Russia-Ukraine conflicts appear to be wrapping up soon.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Plan for elevated refined-product costs indefinitely.

insights.claim: Fuller cites data that the 10-year Treasury yield has risen since the Iran war began, keeping the Fed restrictive and slowing housing.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Geopolitical energy shock transmits to housing through rates.

insights.claim: Fuller says higher transportation prices stem less from diesel and more from reduced truck-driver capacity after the immigration crackdown removed non-compliant carriers and undocumented drivers.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Tight trucking capacity supports freight rates for compliant carriers.

insights.claim: Large trucking companies want stricter driver regulations, and Fuller expects tighter restrictions regardless of who is in office.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Capacity tightness is a durable, bipartisan structural shift benefiting large carriers.
insights.quote: The truckers want stricter regulations and are asking for it and I think they're going to get it regardless who who's in office.

insights.claim: The truck-driver labor pool has reverted to the demographics of 20-30 years ago with no new entrants, which Fuller calls the biggest change in trucking in decades; insurers are also restricting hiring.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Persistent driver shortage underpins rates and favors incumbents.

insights.claim: Fuller estimates ubiquitous self-driving trucks are still 8 to 10 years away.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Autonomy won't relieve the driver shortage in the near term.
insights.quote: we're still 8 to 10 years out before we have ubiquity on self-driving trucks.

insights.claim: Fuller predicts AI data centers and AI automation will become a major election issue in 2028, and job losses from AI could become the most important topic by 2032.
insights.speaker: Craig Fuller (FreightWaves CEO)
insights.so_what: Political backlash risk to AI and data centers rises over the decade.

themes.theme: Market positioning: rotation, defense and precious metals

insights.claim: New Harbor's sector-rotation data shows industrials strong for about two years (added fall 2024, ahead of freight data), but they have lost relative strength in the past couple of months; consumer cyclicals and staples have long lagged.
insights.speaker: John Lohr (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Stocks led the freight data; industrial momentum fading is a caution flag.

insights.claim: Semiconductors have weakened in recent weeks while software, previously called a dead sector due to AI, has performed relatively stronger, which Lohr sees as an early possible sign of AI-theme fatigue.
insights.speaker: John Lohr (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Watch semis-vs-software relative strength as an AI cycle indicator.

insights.claim: Mike Preston says New Harbor's model cut equity exposure from 50% to about 39.5% after stopping out of regional banks, real estate and equal-weight S&P, as a narrow tech-only market triggered warning signs.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Systematic managers are de-risking amid narrow leadership.

insights.claim: Preston notes new leadership emerging in consumer staples (XLP, up ~3% while Nasdaq fell 3%), financials (XLF) and healthcare (XLV cup-and-handle breakout), but doubts the market can progress or make a blow-off top without tech.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Defensive rotation is underway; broad upside requires tech to stabilize.

insights.claim: Preston believes valuations are 'insane' and not congruent with good index returns, but sees a possible thrust higher followed by exhaustion, potentially catalyzed by midterm certainty or lower oil.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Possible near-term rally but poor long-run index return expectations.

insights.claim: Preston says the precious metals pullback from the January high is about 8-9 months long, similar to 2008-2009 when gold fell ~35% and silver ~50% before doubling-plus into 2011; he believes this is a 2008-type pullback, not a 2011-type top.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Historical analog supports holding metals through the drawdown, unleveraged.

insights.claim: Preston thinks silver could move back up to 70-90 within the next 90 days if the reversal holds, though he calls it 'faith time' and advises against leverage.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Asymmetric upside if support holds, but timing is uncertain.

insights.claim: Taggart attributes precious-metals weakness to high oil prices forcing countries to sell assets to afford imports, plus rising real yields; he notes China's 2026 gold purchases are at a record, blowing out the previous record.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: Lower oil or falling real yields could flip metals from headwind to tailwind.

insights.claim: Lohr notes the S&P 500 is about 50% weighted to technology and communications, so even passive indexers hold concentrated tech gains and are seeking hedging and tax strategies.
insights.speaker: John Lohr (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Index investors carry hidden AI concentration risk.
